text:
Sprawling national parks, ancient historical sites, wild and rugged coastlines, and architectural wonders—you don’t need us to tell you that Spain is home to some of the world’s most spectacular sights. But if you had to whittle Spain’s most impressive wonders down to just seven, which would you end up with? We asked the experts—the editors of CNT Spain—to choose the seven most breathtaking places across the country. Here's what they chose.

7 wonders of Spain

Alhambra, Granada

Getty Images

Alhambra, Granada

Possibly the most iconic monument in all of Spain, this stunning spot has been a pilgrimage spot for centuries. It was the fortress of the Nasrid Sultans (rulers of the last Spanish Muslim Kingdom), but in truth it's more of a small city than a single palace. It's a sight to behold, with its Moorish architecture, sandy-colored walls, and sparkling water features—travelers could spend hours admiring the detail in every corner.

Ribeira Sacra

Getty Images

Ribeira Sacra, Galicia

Dramatic scenery, rolling vineyards, and Instagram-worthy views at every turn, the Ribeira Sacra could be one of Spain’s best lesser-known spots. Cliffs teeter at 1,640 feet, before tumbling down in a flurry of vineyards and walking trails to the rushing rivers and gorges of Sil and Miño. Hikers will uncover Romanesque ruins, ancient forests, crumbling monasteries, and orange groves along their way.

Mezquita de Córdoba

Getty Images

Mezquita de Córdoba, Andalusia

With its stunning archways, red-striped pillars, and ornate ceilings, the Mezquita is one of the world's most unique monuments. Originally built as a basilica, but turned into a mosque in 786 was, before being transformed again in 1236, this time into a cathedral. Awarded World Heritage status in 1984, it's a beautiful blend of Islamic and Christian architecture, with Gothic, Renaissance, and Baroque influences. Visit early in the morning to avoid the crowds, or late at night when a light and sound show highlights the beauty of the building.

Teide National Park

Getty Images

Teide National Park, Tenerife

Sprawled across the middle of this Canary island, Teide National Park is a jaw-dropping land of soaring heights and deep gorges, each as breathtaking as the next. The most impressive is the national park’s namesake, El Teide, a cloud-piercing volcano at around 12,200 feet high—Spain’s tallest peak. Hike up (or get the cable car) for unparalleled views across the island’s volcanic landscape, or book a tour with a guide for star-gazing lessons.

Roman Theatre, Mérida

One for the history buffs—Merida is home to some of the world’s best-preserved Roman sites, including the Roman Theatre. This UNESCO World Heritage City was built between 16 and 15 BCE, yet remains one of Spain’s most important archaeological sites. It was designed to seat around 5,000 people and is still famous for its acoustic potential.

Bardenas Reales

Getty Images

Bardenas Reales, Navarra

Picture a desert, and likely images of the Sahara or Gobi spring to mind. But in Spain, the Bardenas Reales offer some of Europe's most spectacular desert landscapes. Stretching out across more than 100,000 acres, this UNESCO-protected nature reserve is the perfect destination for adventure-loving travelers, with off-road trails, mountain biking, and hiking tours.

Cabo de Gata, Almería

This sun-soaked coastline is home to some of Spain's best beaches—think craggy caves, volcanic rocks, desert landscapes, and miles of sugar-soft sand. The Almería province is often overlooked in favour of more popular Spanish destinations, but the Cabo de Gata nature reserve is a wild and rugged spot that changes drastically with the seasons, from sun-parched, lunar-like stretches in winter to verdant, lush lands in spring.

This article was originally published in Condé Nast Traveller UK.
